meta.name: Pharaoh Hound Grooming Guide
meta.excerpt: The Pharaoh Hound has one of the easiest coats in the dog world — short, fine, and requiring almost no specialized care. A weekly wipe-down and routine nail and ear maintenance covers it.
meta.meta_description: Pharaoh Hound grooming guide: the short fine coat requires minimal work, but ears, nails, and skin care after outdoor activity are the regular maintenance...

intro.label: The Pharaoh Hound Coat
intro.heading: A Coat Built for Speed, Not Fuss
intro.html:
Run a hand down a Pharaoh Hound and you'll notice there's almost nothing there — a single, fine, close-lying layer of hair over lean muscle, with no undercoat to trap dirt, moisture, or odor. This is a sighthound built for open-country running in a Mediterranean climate, and the coat reflects that job: it sheds water and heat quickly, contributes almost nothing to insulation, and requires none of the brushing marathons that owners of double-coated or wool-coated breeds live with. For a Pharaoh Hound owner, the coat itself is the easy part of ownership. What takes more attention is everything the coat exposes — thin, lightly pigmented skin that shows sunburn, scrapes, and irritation almost immediately, and a lean frame with essentially no body fat buffer against cold.

From Puppy Coat to Adult Coat

Unlike breeds that are born with a soft, woolly puppy coat and later "blow" it out for a coarser adult coat, Pharaoh Hound puppies arrive with a version of the same short, fine coat they'll carry for life. There's no dramatic coat-change event to plan around at four or six months old. What does change with age is skin resilience — puppy skin is thinner and more reactive, so early grooming sessions should be gentle, brief, and framed as a positive routine rather than a battle. By the time a Pharaoh Hound reaches full adult size around 12–18 months, the coat has its final texture and the grooming needs are essentially set for the rest of the dog's 11–14 year lifespan.

The Blush Response and What It Tells You

One grooming-adjacent quirk unique to this breed is the blush — when a Pharaoh Hound is excited, happy, or aroused, blood flow increases to the nose leather and inner ear skin, both of which are hairless and lightly pigmented, and the area visibly flushes rose-pink. It's a charming trait owners bring up constantly, but it's also functionally useful during grooming: because that skin is normally visible and its healthy color is well known to the owner, any dullness, redness that doesn't fade, flaking, or swelling in that same skin stands out quickly. A weekly hands-on session is as much a skin check as a coat wipe-down for this breed.

Tools Worth Owning

  • Rubber curry mitt or chamois cloth ($8–$15) — the main tool, used weekly to lift dead hair and buff the coat to its natural shine.
  • Soft bristle brush ($10–$18, optional) — for a finishing pass after the mitt; not strictly necessary on this coat type.
  • Nail clipper or cordless grinder ($15–$40) — essential; see nail notes below.
  • Cotton balls and a gentle ear cleanser formulated for dogs ($10–$15) — for the weekly prick-ear check.
  • Mild shampoo for short, fine coats ($10–$20 per bottle, lasts several months at this bathing frequency).
  • Dog-safe sunscreen ($12–$18) — a genuinely useful item for this breed, not a novelty.
  • A well-fitted, core-covering dog coat ($30–$70) — cold-weather equipment, covered in more detail below.

Total starter investment runs roughly $85–$180, and because the coat doesn't mat, doesn't need de-shedding tools, and rarely justifies professional grooming visits, that kit lasts for years with only shampoo and sunscreen needing periodic replacement. One quiet advantage of this breed's lean, athletic build: there are no heavy skin folds around the face, neck, or tail to trap moisture and bacteria, so the fold-cleaning routine that wrinkled breeds require simply doesn't apply here.

care.label: Regular Routine
care.heading: Building the Weekly and Monthly Rhythm
care.html:
The Weekly Five Minutes

  • Coat wipe-down. Run the rubber mitt from neck to tail and down each leg. It takes about five minutes and does most of the shedding-control work for the entire week.
  • Ear check. The Pharaoh Hound's upright, prick ears get better natural airflow than the pendulous ears of hound breeds like Bassets or Beagles, so infection risk is genuinely lower — but a weekly glance and wipe with a gentle cleanser still catches early wax buildup or irritation before it becomes a vet visit.
  • Paw and skin pass. This is where the breed's thin skin matters most. After any run, lure-coursing session, or off-leash outing, check pads for cracking and check the body generally for scrapes, thorn punctures, or brush burns — a lean sighthound covering ground at speed through scrub or fencing can pick up small injuries that go unnoticed under a full coat but are obvious on this one.

Monthly (or Every 4–6 Weeks)

  • Bath. Use lukewarm water and a mild, short-coat-formulated shampoo. Lather once, since this coat doesn't hold much dirt, and rinse thoroughly — thin, fine hair shows leftover shampoo residue as dullness or flaking far more obviously than a thick coat would hide it.
  • Dry. A towel dry is usually sufficient; the coat has almost no undercoat to hold moisture, so it air-dries in well under an hour indoors. Avoid drying outdoors below 50°F — a wet, coatless dog chills fast.
  • Nail trim. An active, running dog wears its nails down somewhat, but rarely enough on its own — plan on a trim or grind every 2–4 weeks. Long nails change how a sighthound's foot strikes the ground and can affect gait and comfort over a lifetime of running.
  • Teeth. A few brushings a week with an enzymatic dog toothpaste is worth the two minutes; dental disease is common across all breeds and easy to prevent early.

Sun and Skin: The Real Grooming Risk for This Breed

Because the coat is so sparse and the skin underneath is lightly pigmented, the nose and ear leather — the same areas that blush pink — are genuinely vulnerable to sunburn during long, sun-intense days, particularly in summer or at altitude. Dog-safe sunscreen applied before extended outdoor time is a reasonable habit, not overcaution. Watch for peeling, redness that lingers after the dog has calmed down, or sensitivity to touch on the nose bridge; these are signs of sun damage, not blush, and worth addressing with shade, sunscreen, or a vet visit if persistent.

DIY vs. Professional Grooming

Most Pharaoh Hound owners never need a professional groomer for the coat itself — there's little a groomer does that a $10 mitt and a bathtub don't already accomplish. Where owners do sometimes use a groomer is for nail trims on a dog that's difficult to handle at home, or an occasional bath before a show or event.

ServiceTypical CostFrequency
Home bath and wipe-down$10–$20 in suppliesEvery 4–6 weeks
Professional bath only$30–$50As needed, optional
Nail trim by a groomer or vet tech$10–$20Every 3–4 weeks if not done at home

Grooming Mistakes This Breed's Owners Actually Make

  • Assuming the easy coat means no maintenance at all. Skipping the weekly check because the coat looks fine leads to missed sunburn, small wounds, or ear irritation that would otherwise be caught early.
  • Over-bathing a coat that doesn't need it. Because bathing is quick and easy, some owners do it weekly "just because." That's more often than this coat and skin type need, and it dries out skin that's already thin.
  • Reaching for undercoat rakes or de-shedding tools. There is no undercoat to remove; these tools are unnecessary and can irritate skin on a single-layer coat.
  • Skipping sunscreen entirely. Owners used to thinking of sunburn as a human problem overlook it in a breed with genuinely exposed, lightly pigmented skin on the nose and ears.
  • Assuming running wears nails down enough. It helps, but active dogs still need scheduled trims — overgrown nails on a sighthound affect running mechanics more than on a low-energy breed.

special.label: Cold Weather and Seasonal Care
special.heading: Managing a Coat That Offers Almost No Insulation
special.html:
The single biggest grooming-adjacent management issue for the Pharaoh Hound isn't the coat's upkeep — it's the coat's near-total lack of insulation. With minimal body fat, a lean athletic build, and a coat that's essentially a single thin layer, this breed feels cold in conditions many other dogs shrug off. Below about 50°F, a well-fitted dog coat that covers the chest, belly, and back is appropriate for any outdoor activity, and below freezing, outdoor time should be purposeful and brief rather than leisurely. This is not a dog that can be left outside for extended periods in cold weather, and sleeping arrangements should always be indoors, ideally in a draft-free spot with a bed offering some cushioning for a lean frame with little natural padding.

Cold-Weather Gear Checklist

ItemPurposeApproximate Cost
Core-covering fleece or quilted coatDaily cold-weather walks, 50°F and below$30–$70
Waterproof outer layerRain or wet snow conditions$35–$80
Paw balm or waxProtecting thin paw skin from ice and salt$10–$18
Indoor bed with bolstered sidesDraft protection and joint cushioning$40–$100

A Year in the Life of the Coat

Spring and summer: This is the season of most concern for skin exposure rather than coat volume — longer daylight and more outdoor running time, whether on-leash walks or lure coursing (an excellent, breed-appropriate outlet for the prey drive that this breed genuinely needs alongside its 60–90 minutes of daily exercise), mean more sun exposure on the nose and ears and more opportunity for scrapes from brush and rough ground. Sunscreen and post-run skin checks matter more in these months than any brushing routine.

Fall: Coat needs stay essentially flat, but this is the season to check that cold-weather gear still fits and hasn't worn out over the previous winter, before temperatures drop.

Winter: The coat itself doesn't thicken to compensate for cold the way a double coat would, so all cold management is external — coats, shortened but purposeful outdoor sessions, indoor sleeping, and attentiveness to ice and de-icing salts, which are irritating to the thin-skinned paws of a sighthound built with almost no protective padding. Wipe paws after walks on treated sidewalks.

Because there's no true undercoat to shed seasonally, owners shouldn't expect the dramatic, week-long shedding surges that double-coated breeds go through each spring and fall. Hair loss stays light and fairly constant year-round, and the weekly mitt session is generally enough to keep it off furniture and clothing regardless of season.

When to Call the Vet Instead of Reaching for a Grooming Tool

Because this breed's skin is so visible and reactive, it's tempting to treat every redness as a grooming issue to be brushed or bathed away. Persistent redness that isn't the normal blush, flaking that doesn't resolve with a milder shampoo, thickened or cracked paw pads, or a nose that stays raw and peeling after sun exposure are all reasons to involve a veterinarian rather than continuing a home routine. A lean, thin-skinned athletic breed shows problems on the surface faster than many others — that's an advantage for early detection, as long as the signs are taken seriously rather than groomed over.

faq.q: How often should a Pharaoh Hound actually be bathed?
faq.a: Roughly every 4 to 6 weeks, or sooner if the dog gets visibly dirty after a run or a muddy field session. Because there's no undercoat to hold odor or debris, this coat simply doesn't need frequent washing the way longer or double coats do. Bathing more often than that strips natural oils from skin that's already thin and lightly pigmented, which can leave the coat looking dull and the skin feeling dry or flaky rather than helping.

faq.q: Does the Pharaoh Hound shed a lot?
faq.a: Very little. With no undercoat and only a single fine layer of hair, this breed loses hair steadily but lightly year-round rather than going through the dramatic seasonal shedding events that double-coated breeds experience twice a year. A weekly pass with a rubber grooming mitt catches most of what does come loose, and most owners describe hair on furniture as a minor, manageable issue rather than a daily chore.

faq.q: Does my Pharaoh Hound really need a dog coat in winter?
faq.a: Yes — this is one of the more genuine cold-weather-gear requirements among dog breeds. With almost no body fat and a coat that offers little insulation, a Pharaoh Hound gets cold quickly below about 50°F, and shivering on a walk isn't a minor quirk, it's a sign the dog is uncomfortable. A well-fitted coat covering the chest, belly, and back should go on before outdoor activity in cool weather, and the dog should sleep indoors year-round.

faq.q: Why does my Pharaoh Hound's nose turn pink, and is that a grooming concern?
faq.a: The pink flush on the nose and inner ear leather is the breed's well-known blush response — increased blood flow to hairless, lightly pigmented skin when the dog is excited or happy. It's normal and not a health issue on its own. It becomes relevant to grooming because that same visible skin is where sunburn and irritation also show up first, so knowing your dog's normal blush helps you notice when redness lingers for the wrong reasons, such as sun exposure or a skin reaction.

faq.q: Do I need to worry about sunburn during grooming or outdoor time?
faq.a: More than most breeds, yes. The Pharaoh Hound's coat is thin and the skin beneath it, especially on the nose and ears, is lightly pigmented and can burn during long, sun-intense outings. Applying a dog-safe sunscreen before extended time outside, especially in summer, and checking the nose and ear leather for peeling or persistent redness after sun exposure, are reasonable and worthwhile habits rather than overcaution for this particular breed.
